     Interactive Entertainment LLC, (“Defendant”, “Sony”). Plaintiffs allege the following upon

 4              1.      Plaintiffs bring this class action complaint against Sony for its retention of a
 5   substantial windfall generated by unlawful tariffs imposed by the federal government under the
 6
     International Emergency Economic Powers Act (“IEEPA”), 50 U.S.C. § 1701, et seq.
 7
                2.      Beginning in February 2025, the Trump administration imposed sweeping tariffs
 8

 9
10   dramatically increased the cost of imported consumer goods sold in the United States.

11              3.      Major U.S. importers, including Sony, responded by increasing prices on consumer
12   goods to offset the cost of these tariffs. As a result, consumers in the U.S. paid higher retail prices
13
     for goods reflecting the economic burden of these tariffs.
14
                4.      Plaintiffs are such consumer. Plaintiffs purchased a Sony PlayStation Console with
15

16
17   5 Digital Edition on December 1, 2025, and Plaintiff Bryce Foster-Quarles purchased a paid a

18   PlayStation 5 Digital Edition on February 20, 2026. Upon information and belief, the price

19   Plaintiffs paid for the PlayStations was higher due to Defendant passing on the cost of IEEPA
20   tariffs.
21
                5.      On February 20, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court held that President Trump’s IEEPA-
22
     based tariffs are unlawful. Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, 607 U.S.        (2026) (slip op. at 20).
23
                6.      Resulting from that decision, importers who paid those IEEPA-based tariffs –
24
25   including Sony – became entitled to refunds of the duties they previously paid to U.S. Customs

26   and Border Protection (“CBP”). To facilitate the refunds to thousands of U.S. importers – including

27

     Sony – the CBP created a tariff refund website to manage IEEPA duty refunds following the
 1
 2   Supreme Court’s February 20, 2026, Learning Resources, Inc. decision.

 3          7.      The economic reality of the tariff regime, however, is that importers like Sony did

 4   not ultimately bear all the costs of the tariffs. Sony, for instance, passed the elevated costs on to
 5   U.S. consumers in the form of higher retail prices on one popular product, the Sony PlayStation,
 6
     beginning on August 21, 2025.
 7

 8

 9
10          9.      Unless restrained by this Court, Sony stands to recover the same tariff payments

11   twice – once from consumers through higher prices and again from the federal government through
12   tariff refunds, including interest paid by the government on those refunds.
13

14

15

16
17          12.     Plaintiffs bring this class action on behalf of thousands, if not millions, of U.S.

18   consumers who purchased Sony’s PlayStation Consoles during the tariff period and who paid

19   inflated prices reflecting Sony’s pass-through of unlawful tariffs.

21

22

26   International Emergency Economic Powers Act (“IEEPA”). The purchase price for the goods that

 1

 5           20.        Sony Interactive Entertainment LLC’s parent company, Sony Group Corporation,
 6

 7

10   (“Sony” or “Defendant”) is the global business behind the well-known PlayStation brand,

11   responsible for the development, production, and sales of both hardware and software. Sony’s most
12   recent model, the PlayStation 5, has become the best-selling video game console of all time. The
13

16
17           22.        Sony currently produces the PlayStation 5, PlayStation 5 Pro, PlayStation 5 Slim,

18   and PlayStation 5 Slim Digital Edition (the “PlayStation Consoles”).

22

     Consoles in the U.S.

 9
10   imports from Canada and Mexico, tariffs as high as 145% from China, and a baseline 10% tariff

11   on nearly all imports to the United States.

13
     tariffs had a substantial impact on the cost of Sony PlayStation Consoles, which are imported from
14

16
17   the tariffs impacted Sony’s PlayStation Console production in China, and required Sony to pay

18   nearly $194 million in import-related fees during the July-September 2025 quarter.

19            30.      Economists and government agencies widely recognize that tariffs are largely borne
20   by domestic consumers rather than foreign exporters or the importing firms that formally remit the
21
     duties. Economic studies examining recent U.S. tariff regimes consistently find that the cost of
22
     tariffs is passed through into higher prices paid by U.S. purchasers of imported goods. 2
23
24
25

26   19, 2026); see also Mary Amiti, Stephen J. Redding & David Weinstein, The Impact of the 2018–2019 Tariffs on
     Prices and Welfare, 135 J. Econ. Persp. 187 (2020).

28

             31.      When tariffs increase the cost of imported goods, retailers and other downstream
 1
 2   sellers typically raise prices to offset those additional costs. Surveys of U.S. businesses conducted

 3   by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York during the recent tariff period found that a large

 4   majority of firms facing tariff-related cost increases passed at least some portion of those costs
 5   through to their customers in the form of higher prices.3 Companies consider tariffs to be costs that
 6
     are to be incorporated into the pricing structure.

             32.      Sony was no exception. Like other companies that faced the massive IEEPA tariffs,
 8
     Sony raised its PlayStation Consoles’ prices on August 21, 2025, and then again on April 2, 2026.
 9
10           33.      Citing inflation and global economic pressures, Sony passed the elevated tariff

11   costs on to U.S. consumers in the form of higher retail prices. To offset its substantial tariff bill,
12   on August 21, 2025, Sony raised prices for all versions of the PlayStation Consoles to be sold in
13
     the U.S. by $50. Then, on March 27, 2026, Sony announced it will raise prices once again on its

19   sales price of the PlayStation 5 Pro, Sony’s most powerful version of the console, increased by

21
             34.      On February 20, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court held that the IEEPA tariff regime
22
     was unlawful because the IEEPA does not authorize the President to impose such tariffs; the Court

     thus invalidated all IEEPA-based tariffs. Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, 607 U.S.           (2026)

     conduct, will unjustly retain improperly obtained revenues, or will otherwise escape liability for
